design_detail: Cross-sectional field study in Salt Lake City, Utah. 52 people who had used ecstasy at least 17 times (30 with 17 to 50 episodes, 22 with more than 50) and 59 who had never used it, all from the all-night dance (rave) scene, with strict limits on lifetime use of other drugs and alcohol, and with abstinence and undisclosed drug use checked by breath, urine and hair tests at the testing visit. Battery of 15 neuropsychological tests (40 scored measures in Table 2); linear regression adjusted for age, gender, race/ethnicity, four family-of-origin variables, childhood conduct disorder and childhood ADHD. Designed as a replication, in a fresh sample, of the same group's 2004 pilot study. Read as the accepted author manuscript in PubMed Central.
can_establish: Whether, among people from the same dance scene with minimal exposure to other drugs and alcohol, a history of ecstasy use of the size reported here (median 43.5 episodes) goes with detectable differences on a broad cognitive battery at least 25 days after last use, and which large differences can be ruled out for heavier use.
cannot_establish: Whether ecstasy causes or does not cause cognitive change (no testing before use); the effects of much heavier use (only 6 people reported 150 or more episodes); differences of medium size on most measures (not excluded for heavier use on 8 of 14 measures); or results in people who use ecstasy together with other drugs, who are most people who use it.

sample.recruitment: Case finders advertised at raves and other places frequented by the Salt Lake City all-night dance scene; telephone screening included irrelevant questions to hide the criteria, and people turned down were not told why (Materials and Methods › Participants, 1st and 2nd paragraphs). About 1500 people screened by telephone, about 250 qualified for the baseline visit, 116 met all criteria and completed testing, and 5 were excluded for drugs found in hair or urine (Results, 1st paragraph). Payment: $100 for the baseline visit, $100 for testing and $150 after the urine and hair results were confirmed (Neuropsychological Testing Visit, 5th paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Aged 18 to 45; at least 17 lifetime episodes of ecstasy use or none; native English speakers; at least 10 all-night dance parties (awake until at least 4:30 AM). Excluded: more than 100 lifetime episodes of cannabis use or more than 10 of any other illicit drug class, more than 50 lifetime episodes of alcohol intoxication, clinically significant head injury or medical illness affecting cognition, and current psychoactive medication; psychiatric disorders were not excluded (Participants, 2nd paragraph). The criteria were relaxed for 6 people near the end (cocaine 15 and 20 times; other hallucinogens 11, 14 and 22 times; cannabis 250 times) (Results, 1st paragraph).
sample.demographics: Comparison group vs ecstasy group (Table 1): men 64.4% vs 57.7% (p = 0.56); white 91.5% vs 76.9% (p = 0.04); father's education high school or less 27.1% vs 53.9% (p = 0.006), mother's 27.1% vs 61.5% (p < 0.001); parents' income $30,000 or less 27.1% vs 30.8%; median age 24 vs 22 years (p = 0.06); current major depression 6.8% vs 5.8%; current anxiety disorder 15.3% vs 9.6%.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single testing). Of about 1500 people screened, 111 were analysed; the characteristics of those not tested are not reported.
sample.selection_effects: A highly selected sample: people who used ecstasy with little other drug or alcohol use, chosen from a dance scene with a comparison group from the same scene. The ecstasy group had attended more all-night parties (median 98 vs 45, p = 0.005), more often had parents with little education, and had lower vocabulary scores (Table 1; Table 2). Exposure was modest (median 43.5 episodes).

exposure.measurement: Semi-structured interview on lifetime episodes, doses and settings of ecstasy use and lifetime use of alcohol and other drugs (Baseline Evaluation). At testing: breathalyzer and urine dipstick (cannabis, opioids, cocaine, barbiturates, amphetamines, benzodiazepines, phencyclidine), exclusion if positive; urine sent to an outside laboratory for MDMA; hair (or axillary hair) tested for drugs over the past 90 days; results discarded if urine was positive for MDMA or hair positive for a drug the person had denied (Neuropsychological Testing Visit, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Lifetime ecstasy episodes median 43.5 (interquartile range 27 to 87.3) (Table 1); groups of 17 to 50 and more than 50 episodes (Statistical Analyses, 1st paragraph); only 6 people reported 150 or more episodes (Discussion, 6th paragraph). Amounts per episode were collected but are not reported. Tablet content unknown.
exposure.polysubstance: Kept low by the exclusion limits and checked by breath, urine and hair tests; residual differences in Table 1: lifetime marijuana intoxications median 10 (interquartile range 4 to 30) vs 1 (0 to 6), p < 0.001; cigarettes a day median 0 in both, p = 0.04; lifetime alcohol intoxications 10 vs 10. Marijuana use was not among the adjustment variables; a repeat analysis without the 6 people over the drug limits gave very similar results (Results, 2nd paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: At least 10 days without ecstasy, other illicit drugs or all-night parties required before testing (Neuropsychological Testing Visit, 1st paragraph); observed minimum 25 days since last ecstasy use, 3 people (6%) under 40 days, median 121 days (interquartile range 60 to 209) (Results, 2nd paragraph; Table 1).

comparison.controls: 59 people who had never used ecstasy, from the same dance scene (at least 10 all-night parties), under the same exclusion limits.
comparison.matching: Not individually matched; adjusted by linear regression for age, gender, race/ethnicity, parents' combined education, parents' income, family history of psychiatric disorder, family history of substance use disorder, childhood conduct disorder and childhood ADHD score (Statistical Analyses, 1st paragraph). Verbal IQ and current depression scores were added only in a check of the strategy-application result.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No testing before ecstasy use. Vocabulary and verbal IQ, which the authors treat as signs of premorbid ability, were lower in the ecstasy group (Table 2); childhood ADHD and conduct disorder were assessed retrospectively.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Minimal by design (lifetime marijuana intoxications median 1; alcohol intoxications median 10).

outcomes.instruments: WAIS-R Vocabulary, Digit Span, Digit Symbol and Block Design; Rey-Osterrieth Complex Figure; Wisconsin Card Sorting Test; Trail Making A and B; Raven's Progressive Matrices; FAS verbal fluency; Stroop; California Verbal Learning Test, second edition; WMS-III Logical Memory, Verbal Paired Associates and Spatial Span; Revised Strategy Application Test; computerized Iowa Gambling Task; Grooved Pegboard; plus the Beck Depression Inventory (Neuropsychological Testing Visit, 4th paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: No comparison with published norms is reported.
outcomes.operationalization: Adjusted mean differences between groups (non-using minus ecstasy group); no definition of impairment. Equivalence-type bounds (from 90% confidence intervals) for the heavier-use group on 14 chosen measures (Statistical Analyses, 2nd paragraph; Table 4).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None, by stated choice: the authors judge Bonferroni correction too conservative and ask readers to bear multiple testing in mind (Statistical Analyses, 3rd paragraph). 40 counts the measures in Table 2; each was also compared for the two use subgroups (Table 3).

analysis.effect_sizes: Whole ecstasy group vs comparison group, adjusted differences (comparison minus ecstasy group, 95% CI; Table 2): verbal memory near zero, e.g. CVLT trials 1-5 total 61.6 vs 60.6, -0.5 (-4.2 to 3.2), p = 0.79; WMS-III logical memory delayed 31.1 vs 29.4, 0.7 (-2.4 to 3.8), p = 0.65; verbal paired associates delayed 6.8 vs 6.8, 0.1 (-0.7 to 0.8). Significant (uncorrected): vocabulary 52.9 vs 45.8, 4.7 (1.1 to 8.4), p = 0.01; digit symbol 72.7 vs 64.5, 7.1 (1.0 to 13.2), p = 0.02; spatial span forward 9.7 vs 9.0, 0.8 (0.0 to 1.6), p = 0.04; non-dominant-hand pegboard 67.2 vs 72.4 s, -5.0 (-9.3 to -0.7), p = 0.02; borderline Raven's 2.2 (0.0 to 4.3), p = 0.05, and digits backwards 0.9 (0.0 to 1.9), p = 0.05; verbal IQ 108.4 vs 99.3, 6.0 (-0.2 to 12.2), p = 0.06. Heavier use (more than 50 episodes, n = 22) vs comparison group (Table 3): proportion of brief items on the Revised Strategy Application Test 88.5 vs 79.5%, 8.7 (3.1 to 14.4), p = 0.003; non-dominant pegboard 67.2 vs 75.6 s, -8.4 (-13.9 to -2.8), p = 0.003; vocabulary 5.0 (0.2 to 9.8), p = 0.04. 17 to 50 episodes (n = 30): Raven's 3.0 (0.5 to 5.4), p = 0.02; digit symbol 8.4 (1.4 to 15.3), p = 0.02; vocabulary 4.6 (0.4 to 8.8), p = 0.03; WCST categories 0.9 (0.1 to 1.7), p = 0.03; spatial span forward 0.9 (0.0 to 1.8), p = 0.04. Within the ecstasy group, more lifetime episodes (log scale) went with fewer brief items, coefficient -1.4 (-2.3 to -0.4), p = 0.004, Pearson r = -0.37 (Results, 2nd paragraph; Figure 1). Bounds for heavier use (Table 4): the largest Cohen's d not excluded ranged from 0.37 to 0.76. Editors' calculation: adjusted standardized differences for the whole group, about 0.48 for vocabulary, 0.50 for digit symbol and -0.05 for CVLT total; for heavier use about 0.81 for brief items and 0.92 for the pegboard; of the 40 adjusted differences in Table 2, 29 point towards lower performance in the ecstasy group, 8 towards higher and 3 are zero (a count only: the measures are correlated, so this is not a test); in Table 4, medium effects (d 0.5) are excluded on 6 of 14 measures and not on 8.
analysis.covariates: Age, gender, race/ethnicity, parents' education, parents' income, family history of psychiatric disorder, family history of substance use disorder, childhood conduct disorder, childhood ADHD score. Not adjusted for lifetime all-night parties, marijuana use or verbal IQ (verbal IQ and depression score only in a check of the strategy-application result).
analysis.selective_reporting: Tables 2 and 3 are titled representative test scores, without saying whether every scored variable is shown. Several checks are reported only in words: the simplified model and the analysis without the 6 people over the drug limits (very similar), the strategy-application result adjusted for verbal IQ and depression (virtually unchanged), and the exploratory analyses behind calling the pegboard difference chance (not shown) (Results, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 1st paragraph). The equivalence bounds cover 14 measures chosen for the heavier-use group only (Table 4).
analysis.power: No power calculation. The equivalence bounds (Table 4) show what the comparison of 22 people with heavier use and 59 without could exclude: Cohen's d of 0.8 or more on all 14 chosen measures, and of 0.5 or more on 6 of them (editors' count).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Adjusted differences were small and mostly non-significant across 40 measures, including all verbal-memory measures; the significant differences (uncorrected) were lower vocabulary, digit symbol and spatial span and a slower non-dominant hand in the whole ecstasy group, and fewer brief strategy items, a slower non-dominant hand and lower vocabulary with heavier use; within the ecstasy group more episodes went with fewer brief items. Most point estimates lean towards lower scores in the ecstasy group.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The authors conclude that they failed to demonstrate marked residual cognitive effects, give both possible readings (a false negative, or that ecstasy by itself does not generally produce lasting residual neurotoxicity) and state that the question remains incompletely resolved (abstract; Discussion, 6th and 7th paragraphs). Each significant difference is set aside as premorbid (vocabulary), chance (differences seen only with lighter use; the pegboard, on analyses not shown) or possibly premorbid impulsivity (strategy application), while non-significant results are read as no difference; the claim that even a medium effect could be excluded on many measures (Results, 3rd paragraph) holds for 6 of 14. The cross-sectional design cannot show that the lower vocabulary predates use.

timeline.event: Pilot study by the same group (23 people who used ecstasy, 16 who did not, minimal other drug use): heavier use (60 to 450 episodes) went with differences in processing speed, strategic self-regulation and executive function, lighter use with almost none (as described in the Introduction, 4th paragraph).

Gouzoulis-Mayfrank and colleagues, 38 people followed over 18 months: those who stopped (17) did not improve and those who continued (21) did not deteriorate (as described in the Discussion, 4th paragraph).
Prospective study of people starting ecstasy use: smaller verbal-memory gains after a median of 1.5 tablets, which this paper says raises doubt about a causal role (Discussion, 4th paragraph).
This study: of the pilot's differences with heavier use, only strategic self-regulation recurred.
Letter re-interpreting these findings as consistent with serotonergic neurotoxicity (title as recorded; not read by this reader).
Commentary on this study (title: strengthening the case against functionally significant serotonergic neurotoxicity; not read by this reader).

replication.where_it_stands: This study is itself the replication of the 2004 pilot, and reproduced only the strategy-application difference with heavier use. It is the main study of people who used ecstasy with minimal other drug use among the papers read in this batch; a published letter and a commentary on it are read separately. No independent replication is described in the papers read here.

funding.declared_conflicts: None of the authors reports conflicts of interest, and none reports support from the tobacco, alcohol, pharmaceutical or gaming industries in association with this study (Footnotes).
funding.affiliations_note: McLean Hospital and Harvard Medical School (Belmont and Boston, Massachusetts); University of New Mexico (Author information). Recorded as a flag for closer reading only.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort of people from the same scene tested before first use, with hair-verified exposure across a wide range including heavy use, a pre-specified primary outcome and an equivalence margin set in advance, so that both the presence and the absence of medium-sized differences can be shown.

domains.note: Many premorbid and family variables adjusted for; residual differences in marijuana use and party attendance not adjusted; lower vocabulary in the ecstasy group may reflect premorbid ability (which would bias towards finding differences) or an effect of use.
Lifetime episodes self-reported and tablet content unknown, but abstinence and undisclosed use of other drugs checked by breath, urine and hair tests.
About 111 of 1500 screened; a deliberately unusual group of people who used ecstasy with little else; characteristics of those excluded not reported.
5 tested people excluded by design for positive drug tests; no other missing data reported.
Standardized tests, but blinding of the tester to group is not reported.
Representative tables, 40 measures without correction, checks reported without numbers, equivalence bounds for chosen measures only.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The design addresses the main confounders of this literature (other drug use, verified abstinence, comparison from the same scene, family and childhood variables), so the small differences are less likely to be explained by polydrug use than in most studies. Concerns remain about residual confounding, unreported tester blinding and selective presentation, and the sample's modest exposure limits what the null results can exclude. The study may be cited for small or absent differences on most tests after moderate ecstasy use with minimal other drug use, and for the exclusion of large differences with heavier use; it may not be cited as showing that ecstasy has no lasting effect, or that medium-sized effects are excluded.

key_findings.finding: Of about 1500 people screened by telephone, about 250 qualified for baseline, 116 completed testing and 5 were excluded for drugs found in hair or urine, leaving 52 people who had used ecstasy and 59 who had not; criteria were relaxed for 6 people.

Ecstasy use: lifetime episodes median 43.5 (interquartile range 27 to 87.3); days since last use median 121 (60 to 209), minimum 25, 3 people under 40; 30 people with 17 to 50 episodes and 22 with more than 50.

The ecstasy group more often had parents with high-school education or less (father 53.9% vs 27.1%, p = 0.006; mother 61.5% vs 27.1%, p < 0.001), was less often white (76.9% vs 91.5%, p = 0.04), had attended more all-night parties (median 98 vs 45, p = 0.005) and reported more marijuana intoxications (median 10 vs 1, p < 0.001).

Memory measures did not differ after adjustment: CVLT trials 1-5 total 61.6 vs 60.6, difference -0.5 (95% CI -4.2 to 3.2), p = 0.79; WMS-III logical memory immediate 0.7 (-3.6 to 5.0) and delayed 0.7 (-2.4 to 3.8); verbal paired associates delayed 0.1 (-0.7 to 0.8); Rey-Osterrieth delayed recall 0.8 (-1.8 to 3.4).

Significant (uncorrected) whole-group differences: vocabulary 4.7 (1.1 to 8.4), p = 0.01; digit symbol 7.1 (1.0 to 13.2), p = 0.02; spatial span forward 0.8 (0.0 to 1.6), p = 0.04; non-dominant-hand pegboard -5.0 s (-9.3 to -0.7), p = 0.02; borderline Raven's (p = 0.05) and digits backwards (p = 0.05); verbal IQ 6.0 (-0.2 to 12.2), p = 0.06.

Heavier use (more than 50 episodes, n = 22) vs no use: fewer brief items on the Revised Strategy Application Test, 79.5 vs 88.5%, difference 8.7 (3.1 to 14.4), p = 0.003, virtually unchanged after further adjustment for verbal IQ and depression score; slower non-dominant-hand pegboard, -8.4 s (-13.9 to -2.8), p = 0.003; lower vocabulary 5.0 (0.2 to 9.8), p = 0.04; no other differences.
key_findings.locator: Table 3 (comparison vs heavier-use columns); Results, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Lighter use (17 to 50 episodes, n = 30) vs no use: lower Raven's 3.0 (0.5 to 5.4), digit symbol 8.4 (1.4 to 15.3), vocabulary 4.6 (0.4 to 8.8), Wisconsin categories 0.9 (0.1 to 1.7) and spatial span forward 0.9 (0.0 to 1.8), p = 0.02 to 0.04; the authors note these appeared with lighter but not heavier use.
key_findings.locator: Table 3 (comparison vs lighter-use columns); Results, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Within the ecstasy group, more lifetime episodes (log-transformed) went with fewer brief items: coefficient -1.4 (-2.3 to -0.4), p = 0.004, adjusted for age, gender and race/ethnicity; Pearson r = -0.37; not driven by outliers on inspection of the scatterplot.
key_findings.note: Figure 1 is an image; values were not read from it.

key_findings.finding: For heavier use vs no use, the largest effect not excluded at the 0.05 level ranged from Cohen's d 0.37 (Wisconsin perseverations) to 0.76 (spatial span total) on 14 chosen measures; the authors say a large effect (d 0.8) could be excluded on all of them and a medium effect (d 0.5) on many.
key_findings.note: Editors' count: d 0.5 is excluded on 6 of the 14 measures (values from 0.37 to 0.50) and not on 8 (0.53 to 0.76).

key_findings.finding: The authors read the lower vocabulary as a premorbid difference, since vocabulary is generally preserved after neurological insults, and the differences seen only with lighter use, and the pegboard difference, as likely chance; strategic self-regulation is their only consistent finding, possibly reflecting reflection impulsivity, which they say may predate use.

The authors note their results conflict with their own pilot, possibly because the pilot's heavier-use group was tested after shorter median abstinence (59.5 vs 121 days), because of unmeasured confounders or by chance.

The authors give two readings: a false negative, perhaps because only 6 participants had 150 or more episodes or few had predisposing factors; or that ecstasy by itself does not generally produce lasting residual neurotoxicity; and they conclude that the question remains incompletely resolved.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results say that even a medium effect (d 0.5 or more) could be excluded on many measures, but by Table 4 a medium effect is excluded on 6 of the 14 chosen measures and not on the other 8 (editors' count).
reporting_issues.consequence: The null results are less informative than the text suggests: medium-sized differences with heavier use remain possible on most measures shown.

reporting_issues.issue: The pegboard difference with heavier use (p = 0.003) is called likely due to chance on the basis of exploratory analyses that are not reported, and several robustness checks are reported only in words.
reporting_issues.consequence: The basis for discounting significant differences cannot be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: The comparison group's SD for the proportion of brief items is 8.8 in Table 2 and 8.7 in Table 3, for the same 59 people.
Tables 2 and 3 are titled representative test scores; whether all scored variables are shown is not stated.
